title: Petra and the Vector
premise: Ulyana Thackeray, a terraformer tending a garden meant for colonists not yet born, maintains an orbital beacon whose original commission has been erased from every record. When the deep-space ship Petra returns with its crew aged backward into childhood, carrying a message that could end the decades-long war between Earth and the Outer Colonies, Ulyana discovers the beacon is a dead-man's switch he himself set in a future that no longer exists — his own memories rewritten by the same temporal field. To deliver the message before the weaponized beacon fires, he must recover who he was, choose between the woman he loves on Earth and the duty encoded in his own past self, and decide whether a peace bought with erased lives is worth anything. In the end he broadcasts the message at the cost of his own timeline, saving the war's end but losing the version of himself that anyone loved — and the child-aged crew of the Petra must grow up again to remember him for him.
about_author: Jonah Okafor is a former hydrologist who spent six years on Antarctic ice-core teams before turning to fiction, a background that seeps into his glacial pacing and obsession with buried time. He writes from Lagos and Reykjavik, whichever city has the longer nights.

chapters.title: The Garden of Unborn Weather
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. On terraformed Kepler-442c, Ulyana tends a seed-vault garden for colonists still in transit and logs another quiet shift maintaining Beacon 7, a structure no archive can explain. The emotional beat is patient loneliness — a man devoted to people who will never know him.

chapters.title: A Ship Older Than Its Crew
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The long-range scope catches the Petra returning fifty years early, transponder codes valid but hull fresh as new paint. Docking reveals a bridge crew of eight-year-olds wearing captain's insignia. Beat: wonder curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Children in Captain's Coats
chapters.summary: Alternating Ulyana and young Commander Ilsa Voss's POV. The children are lucid, articulate, and terrified: they remember being sixty. Their mission log ends mid-sentence at a date that hasn't happened. Beat: uncanny tenderness between caretaker and reversed elders.

chapters.title: The Message That Isn't There Yet
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Ilsa reveals the Petra carries an encrypted message addressed to Beacon 7 specifically — and to 'U.T., who will understand.' Ulyana denies any connection. Beat: denial cracking under evidence.

chapters.title: Records of Nobody
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Digging through colonial archives, Ulyana finds Beacon 7's commissioning file scrubbed so thoroughly the erasure itself is dated three years in the future. Beat: paranoia blooming in a man who trusted his own mind.

chapters.title: What the Garden Remembers
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The children's shared temporal field makes them living recorders; one girl hums a lullaby only Ulyana's late mother knew. Beat: grief and suspicion braided together.

chapters.title: Earth Calls Collect
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. A priority transmission arrives: Earth Command demands the Petra be seized and its message destroyed as enemy propaganda. Among the signatories is Amara Chen, Ulyana's former lover, now a war directorate official. Beat: old love resurfacing as threat.

chapters.title: Amara
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Ulyana's POV. Ten years earlier: Ulyana and Amara on Earth, her rising career, his departure for the frontier, the promise neither kept. Beat: bittersweet nostalgia establishing what duty already cost him once.

chapters.title: The Directorate's Long Arm
chapters.summary: Amara's POV, first time. Aboard the warship Cautious Dawn, Amara argues against destroying the message, suspecting it contains genuine peace terms — and suspects Ulyana is entangled. Her superiors order the beacon armed as a failsafe weapon. Beat: conscience versus chain of command.

chapters.title: Decompression of a Life
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Under the Petra's residual temporal field, fragments surface: Ulyana remembers standing inside Beacon 7, older, setting the dead-man's switch himself. Beat: vertigo of self-betrayal — he may be the enemy's architect or the peace's.

chapters.title: Eight-Year-Old War Council
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The child crew votes, formally, on whether to trust Ulyana with the decryption key. Ilsa casts the deciding vote based on a memory of the older Ulyana she hasn't met yet. Beat: improbable faith.

chapters.title: The Key Is a Name
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The cipher unlocks not to code but to a spoken name — Ulyana's birth name, which he legally abandoned after his mother's death. The message begins playing: terms of surrender drafted by the Outer Colonies' dying leadership. Beat: revelation and responsibility landing at once.

chapters.title: Terms Written by the Dying
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The full message: the Outer Colonies offer unconditional ceasefire if Earth publicly acknowledges the Kessler Atrocity it has denied for thirty years. The children are the last witnesses, aged backward precisely so they'd survive to testify. Beat: moral weight settling onto small shoulders.

chapters.title: Cautious Dawn Arrives
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. The warship enters orbit under orders to seize the Petra and fire Beacon 7's hidden armament — a relativistic kill vehicle aimed at the colonies' capital. Amara stalls, buying hours. Beat: sabotage disguised as diligence.

chapters.title: Two Conversations, One Orbit
chapters.summary: Split POV. Ulyana and Amara speak over an open channel for the first time in a decade, each hiding what they're doing while each trying to save the other. Beat: love against duty made literal in dialogue.

chapters.title: The Dead-Man's Switch Wakes
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Earth's seizure team triggers the beacon's arming sequence; the countdown Ulyana's future self installed begins — seventy-two hours to launch. Beat: trap snapping shut, authored by himself.

chapters.title: Inside My Own Machine
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The children, whose bodies resonate with the temporal field, can enter the beacon's control lattice where adults cannot. Ilsa maps the abort mechanism and finds it requires two keys: command override and the founder's biometric signature. Beat: hope with a terrible price tag.

chapters.title: The Founder's Signature
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The biometric lock reads not present-tense Ulyana but his remembered self — meaning he must genuinely believe in the message's cause for the lock to open. Belief cannot be faked from a machine this intimate. Beat: crisis of conviction.

chapters.title: Seventy-Two Hours
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. Amara openly mutinies, locking the Cautious Dawn's weapons bay and broadcasting the Kessler Atrocity evidence fleet-wide, knowing it ends her career and possibly her life. Beat: duty inverted — loyalty to truth over orders.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, climax. With the countdown at minutes, Ulyana stands in the beacon core, speaks his abandoned name, means it, and turns the kill vehicle into a transmitter: the message and the testimony go out to both fleets simultaneously. Beat: sacrifice of certainty — he acts without knowing if peace will hold.

chapters.title: Ceasefire, With Conditions
chapters.summary: Alternating Amara and Ilsa POV. Fleets stand down; negotiations begin shakily; Amara faces tribunal but public testimony from the child crew shields her. Beat: exhausted, unglamorous relief — peace as process, not fireworks.

chapters.title: The Gardener, Remembered
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV, resolution. Years later, the first colonists arrive to find the garden thriving. The now-grown Petra crew dedicate Beacon 7 — decommissioned, its history restored — to Ulyana Thackeray, who chose to remain partially unrecorded so the message, not the messenger, would carry the weight. Final beat: love outlasting memory; the unborn finally born into his garden.
